key: If you see an intelligent man who tells you where true treasures are to be found, who shows what is to be avoided, and administers reproofs, follow that wise man; it will be better, not worse, for those who follow him.
s: Opening the chapter on the wise man, the verse speaks of whom to follow; the Theravāda commentary, Dhammapada-aṭṭhakathā VI.1, reads it as a charge to take correction without offence, like the pupil Radha, and to look on whoever admonishes as one pointing to treasure.
src: The Theravāda commentary, Dhammapada-aṭṭhakathā VI.1 (on verse 76), trans. Burlingame, Buddhist Legends, vol. 2 (1921), Norman p. 106

opened.edition: E. W. Burlingame, Buddhist Legends, vol. 2, HOS 29 (1921), archive.org buddhistlegends02budd (OCR)
opened.locator: Story VI.1 (Dhammapada 76), A Poor Man Wins Spiritual Treasure, Norman p. 106 (the Teacher, just before the stanza)

evidence.words: Monks, when a fault is pointed out to a monk, he ought to be amenable to discipline like Radha; and when he is admonished, he should not take offense. Indeed he who gives admonition should be looked upon as one who points out where treasures are to be found.
evidence.gloss: Story VI.1: the Teacher, speaking of Radha, who never resented his preceptor Sariputta’s correction, says a monk shown a fault should be amenable like Radha and take no offence, and that one who admonishes is to be looked on as one pointing out treasure; then he speaks verse 76. The Pali Tattha agrees: when such a person points out a fault, kopo na kātabbo, tuṭṭheneva bhavitabbaṃ (no anger is to be shown; one should be glad), as a poor man is glad to be shown treasure.
